The impactor has a name, Theia, and no evidence for its existence beyond the Moon itself. The giant-impact hypothesis only became consensus in the 1980s, largely because nothing else explained why the Moon holds so little iron: a glancing blow would have thrown up Earth's rocky mantle and left both iron cores behind.

The awkward part is the isotopes. Rocks brought back by Apollo match Earth's oxygen isotope ratios almost exactly, when a separate body should have carried a signature of its own. What is not in doubt is that the Moon was once far closer. Laser retroreflectors left on the surface show it receding about 3.8 centimetres a year, and running that backwards puts it over a planet whose day lasted a few hours.
